title: Getting Started
description: Learn how to install and use Paneforge in your projects.
content: Installation  Install Paneforge using your favorite package manager:  npm install paneforge  Basic Usage  Here's a simple example of how to use Paneforge to create a horizontal pane group with two panes:    import { PaneGroup, Pane, PaneResizer } from "paneforge";     Pane 1    Pane 2   The PaneGroup component is used to initialize a pane group, and the Pane component is used to create a pane. The PaneResizer component is used to create a resizer that can be dragged to resize the panes.  The components ship only with the styles necessary to position the panes in the appropriate layout. The rest of the styling is up to you.

title: Introduction
description: What this project is all about.
content: import { NestedGroupsDemo } from '$lib/components/demos'   PaneForge provides components that make it easy to create resizable panes in your Svelte apps. It's designed to be simple to use, and to work well with other Svelte components and libraries. This project has taken a lot of inspiration and code from the work done by $2 and $2 and seeks to provide a similar experience for Svelte developers.  Here's an example of the functionality you can expect from PaneForge:  Features  Simple API**: PaneForge is designed to be easy to use. It provides a small set of components that can be combined to create complex layouts. Resizable Panes**: Panes can be resized by dragging the resizer between them. Nested Groups**: Groups of panes can be nested inside other groups to create complex layouts. Customizable**: The appearance and behavior of the panes can be customized using CSS and Svelte props. Persistent Layouts**: PaneForge can be used with LocalStorage or cookies to persist the layout of the panes between page loads. Accessible**: PaneForge is designed to be accessible to all users, including those who use assistive technologies. Community-driven**: PaneForge is an open-source project that welcomes contributions from the community. If you have an idea for a new feature or an improvement, we'd love to hear from you!  Next Steps  Start using PaneForge in your Svelte app by following the $2 guide. If you have any questions or need help, feel free to ask in the $2!

title: Styling
description: Easily style the various parts of your panes.
content: For each component that renders an HTML element, we expose a class prop that you can use to apply styles to the component. This is the recommended and most straightforward way to style them.  CSS frameworks  If you're using a CSS framework like TailwindCSS or UnoCSS, you can simply pass the classes you need to the component, and they will be applied to the underlying HTML element.    import { Pane } from "paneforge";  Data attributes  A data attribute is applied to each element rendered by PaneForge, which you can use to target the component across your entire application. Check out the API reference of the component to determine what those data attributes are.  You can then use those data attributes like so:  Define global styles  [data-pane-group] {  height: 3rem;  width: 100%;  background-color: #3182ce;  color: #fff; }  Import stylesheet    import "../app.pcss";   let { children } = $props();   {@render children()}  Now every `` component will have the styles applied to it.  Global classes  If you prefer the class approach, you can simply apply your global classes to the component.  1. Define global styles    .pane-group {  height: 3rem;  width: 100%;  background-color: #3182ce;  color: #fff; }  2. Apply global styles      import "../app.pcss";   let { children } = $props();   {@render children()}  3. Use with components      import { PaneGroup } from "paneforge";   Click me  Style Prop  PaneForge components accept a style prop, which will be gracefully merged with the component's internal styles to create a single style string.

title: PaneGroup
description: A container for panes or nested pane groups.
content: import { PropField, Collapsible } from '@svecodocs/kit';   The PaneGroup component wraps a collection of panes or nested PaneGroups and is used to initialize and manage the layout of the panes.  Props   The id to use when storing the layout of the panes in local storage. If provided, the layout will be saved to local storage when it changes. If not provided, the layout will not be saved.     The direction of the panes in the group. If set to 'horizontal', the panes will be arranged side by side. If set to 'vertical', the panes will be arranged one on top of the other.      The unit this group's panes are sized in, for the panes that do not say for themselves. Also the unit keyboardResizeBy is read in.  Set it to size every pane in the group the same way. A single pane needing the other unit says so itself instead of the whole group changing — see $2.      Whether double clicking a resize handle gives every pane in the group the same size. The same thing is available as distributeEvenly(), so you can put it behind your own control instead.      Whether dividers in the groups nested directly inside this one are dragged together when they line up, as one line that goes only as far as all of them can. See $2.     The amount of space to add to the pane group when the keyboard resize event is triggered. If not provided, the default value is used.    void | null" default="null"> A callback that is called when the layout of the panes in the group changes. The layout is an array of numbers representing the size of each pane in pixels.     The storage object to use for saving the layout of the panes in the group.      string | null">    Retrieves the item from storage.       void">    Sets the item to storage.          The underlying DOM element of the pane group. You can bind to this prop to get a reference to the element.      Imperative API for the pane group. bind to this prop to get access to methods for controlling the pane group.     number[]">   Gets the layout of the pane group.     void">   Sets the layout of the pane group.     number">   Gets the size the panes share out: 100 for a percentage group, and the space left over after the resizers for a pixel one.     void">   Gives every pane the same size, holding any pane that cannot take that size at its own limit.     string">   Gets the ID of the pane group. Persisted Layouts/Storage  When the PaneGroup component is provided with an autoSaveId prop, it will automatically save the layout of the panes to local storage. If you want to use a different storage mechanism, you can provide a storage prop with a custom storage object that implements the PaneGroupStorage interface.  export type PaneGroupStorage = {  /** Retrieves the item from storage */  getItem(name: string): string | null;  /** Sets the item to storage */  setItem(name: string, value: string): void; };  Data Attributes  The following data attributes are available for the PaneGroup component:  export type PaneGroupAttributes = {  /** Applied to every pane group element. */  "data-pane-group": "";  /** The direction of the pane group. */  "data-direction": "horizontal" | "vertical";  /** The ID of the pane group. */  "data-pane-group-id": string;  /** The unit the group's panes are sized in unless they say for themselves. */  "data-units": "percentage" | "pixels"; }; `

title: PaneJunctions
description: Renders a draggable handle wherever perpendicular resizers meet, resizing both at once.
content: import { PropField } from '@svecodocs/kit'   A junction is a point where two resizers that move along opposing axes meet. Dragging one moves every resizer that meets there, so a nested layout can be resized in both directions at the same time.  The PaneJunctions component finds those points for you and renders an element for each one.  Usage  Put it anywhere inside the outermost group you want covered. It renders nothing itself, so its position in the markup does not matter. It looks at every group nested within that one, however deep, so a single instance is usually all you need.    import { PaneGroup, Pane, PaneResizer, PaneJunctions } from "paneforge";            One        Three                Two        Four How junctions are found  Junctions are worked out from where the resizers actually sit on screen, not from how the components are arranged. Two resizers form a junction when they touch, no matter how far apart their groups are in the tree — a resizer six levels down meets one in the outermost group just the same as two siblings would.  That also means junctions appear and disappear as the layout changes. Two nested resizers lined up on either side of an outer one form a single cross; drag one out of line and it becomes two separate tees, one at the end of each.  Only resizers that genuinely line up are driven together. Junctions that merely sit near one another stay independent, so dragging one never moves the other. Where their hit areas overlap, the one later in paint order takes the pointer — crossTolerance controls where that line falls.  Where junctions render  Of the resizers meeting at a junction, one runs straight through it while the others stop against it. The junction is rendered inside the one that runs through, for two reasons: it lies entirely within that resizer, so nothing clips it, and flex has already placed that resizer across the junction. Only the distance along its length has to be measured.  That resizer becomes position: relative so the junction can be positioned against it. Resizers that anchor nothing are left alone, including ones that take part in a junction without being the one it runs through.  Junctions are given z-index: 1, because resizers are commonly given position: relative and a later one would otherwise paint over a junction rendered inside an earlier one. If your own handles use a z-index, raise the junction to match.  data-junction-axis says which way the resizer it sits in runs, and data-junction-side says which side the others arrive from — absent on a cross, which is met from both. Together they tell you which way a tee points.  /* a tee met only from the left */ $2[data-junction-side="start"] {  border-left: none; }  If a resizer uses its own child snippet it no longer renders an element for the junctions to live in, so render the junctions snippet it is given inside whatever element takes its place:    {#snippet child({ props, junctions })}           {@render junctions()}     {/snippet}  Dragging as one line  The resizers a junction moves along one axis all meet it at the same point, so they are moved as one: every move is offered to each of them, and they all move by the smallest share any of them could manage. A column whose pane has reached its minSize is where the whole line stops, rather than the other columns running on and leaving the line broken in two.  The two axes are independent of one another. One axis running out of room does not hold the other back.  Evening out  Double clicking a junction gives every pane it can move the same size, which is the same thing $2 does for a single resizer — applied to every group the junction drags, so a crossing evens out along both axes at once.  It follows the same opt-in: groups that have asked for it are evened out and groups that have not are left as they are. If none of them have, the double click is left alone to be handled wherever you like.  Accessibility  Every resizer a junction drives is already exposed on its own as a separator that can be moved with the keyboard. A junction is a pointer shortcut for those same resizers rather than a second route to them, so it is aria-hidden and stays out of the tab order. Keyboard users resize each axis with the resizers themselves.  Props    Whether the junctions are disabled. The resizers they would drive stay usable on their own.      How close, in pixels, resizers must come to count as meeting.      How close, in pixels, two parallel resizers must line up before the junctions they form become a single cross that drags them together.  Deliberately tight: junctions that only sit near each other stay independent. Raise it to make crosses easier to form, and to snap nearby splits together as they are dragged.     void">  A callback that is called when a junction's dragging state changes.  Snippet Props  Both the child and children snippets receive the junction being rendered:  export type PaneJunction = {  /** A stable id derived from the resizers the junction drives. */  id: string;  /** The center of the junction, in viewport coordinates. */  x: number;  y: number;  /** The size of the junction, matching the resizers it crosses. */  width: number;  height: number;  /** Whether resizers meet the junction on both sides, or only one. */  type: "cross" | "tee";  /**   Paint order. Where two junctions in the same resizer overlap, the higher index takes   the pointer.   */  index: number;  /** The resizer it is rendered inside, how far along it, and which side it is met from. */  anchor: {   resizerId: string;   axis: "x" | "y";   offset: number;   side: "start" | "end" | undefined;  };  /** Whether the junction is currently being dragged. */  isDragging: boolean;  /** The ids of the resizers the junction drives, per axis. */  resizerIds: { x: string[]; y: string[] }; };  Data Attributes  The following data attributes are available on each junction element:  export type PaneJunctionAttributes = {  /** Applied to every junction element. */  "data-pane-junction": "";  /** The ID of the junction. */  "data-pane-junction-id": string;  /** The ID of the group owning the resizer the junction is rendered in. */  "data-pane-group-id": string;  /** Whether resizers meet the junction on both sides, or only one. */  "data-junction-type": "cross" | "tee";  /** The axis the resizer it is anchored to travels along. */  "data-junction-axis": "x" | "y";  /** Which side the resizers that stop here arrive from. Absent on a cross. */  "data-junction-side"?: "start" | "end";  /** Whether the junction is being dragged. */  "data-active"?: "pointer";  /** Whether the junction is enabled or not. */  "data-enabled"?: boolean; }; `

title: PaneResizer
description: A draggable handle between two panes that allows the user to resize them.
content: import { PropField, Collapsible } from '@svecodocs/kit'   The PaneResizer component is used to create a draggable handle between two panes that allows the user to resize them.  Usage    import { PaneGroup, Pane, PaneResizer } from "svelte-pane";     Pane 1    Pane 2  Props   Whether the resize handle is disabled.    void"> A callback that is called when the resize handle's dragging state changes.     The underlying DOM element of the pane group. You can bind to this prop to get a reference to the element.  Child Snippet  The child snippet lets you render your own element for the resize handle. It receives the handle's props, along with a junctions snippet holding any $2 anchored to this resizer. Render it inside your element so they are positioned correctly — you can leave it out if you aren't using PaneJunctions.    {#snippet child({ props, junctions })}           {@render junctions()}     {/snippet}   It also receives getLinkedIds(), which returns the ids of the resizers that would be dragged along with this one because they line up with it — see $2. Dividers are linked by where they currently are, so it is measured when called rather than held onto:    {#snippet child({ props, junctions, getLinkedIds })}       (lit = [id, ...getLinkedIds()])}    onmouseleave={() => (lit = [])}    {@render junctions()}     {/snippet}  Data Attributes  The following data attributes are available for the PaneResizer component:  export type PaneResizerAttributes = {  /** The direction of the pane group the handle belongs to. */  "data-direction": "horizontal" | "vertical";  /** The ID of the pane group the handle belongs to. */  "data-pane-group-id": string;  /** Whether the resize handle is active or not. */  "data-active"?: "pointer" | "keyboard";  /** Whether the resize handle is enabled or not. */  "data-enabled"?: boolean;  /** The ID of the resize handle. */  "data-pane-resizer-id": string;  /** Present on all resizer elements */  "data-pane-resizer": ""; }; `

title: Pane
description: An individual pane within a pane group.
content: import { PropField, Collapsible } from '@svecodocs/kit';   The Pane component is used to create an individual pane within a PaneGroup.  Sizes  Every size on a pane is read in its own units: a share of the group by default, or pixels when the pane is set to units="pixels". Panes of both kinds can sit in the same group.  A size can also name its own unit, as minSize="180px" or maxSize="60%", which is read in that unit whatever the pane is sized in. A limit in pixels is the same limit wherever the pane sits, so a pane that takes a share of the group can still refuse to go below the width its contents need. See $2.  Props    The unit this pane is sized in, which is the unit every size on it is read in — defaultSize, minSize, maxSize, collapsedSize, and the sizes reported by onResize and getSize.  A percentage pane takes a share of the group, so it follows the group as it resizes. A pixels pane is absolute: it keeps its size when the group changes size, and the difference is taken up by the panes sizing themselves as a share.     The size of the pane when it is in a collapsed state, in the pane's own units.    Whether the pane can be collapsed.     The size the pane starts at, in its own units, or in the unit it names. Leave it off and the pane takes an even share of whatever the panes that do have one have not claimed, which is how you say "fill the space left over".     The largest the pane may be, in its own units, or in the unit it names.     The smallest the pane may be, in its own units, or in the unit it names.  A limit in pixels does not move with the group, so the same pane has the same smallest size however deeply it is nested. A limit given as a share moves with the group instead.  It is also applied as a min-width or min-height on the pane, so flexbox holds it there to the exact pixel. Collapsible panes are left out of that, since they have to be able to reach their collapsedSize.     The order of the pane in the group. Useful for maintaining order when conditionally rendering panes.    void"> A callback that is called when the pane is collapsed.    void"> A callback that is called when the pane is expanded.    void"> A callback that is called when the pane is resized.     The underlying DOM element of the pane group. You can bind to this prop to get a reference to the element.      Imperative API for the pane group. bind to this prop to get access to methods for controlling the pane group.     void">   Collapse the pane to its minimum size.     void">   Expand the pane to its previous size.     string">   Gets the ID of the pane.     number">   Gets the size of the pane.     boolean">   Checks if the pane is collapsed.     boolean">   Checks if the pane is expanded.     void">   Resize the pane to the specified size. Data Attributes  The following data attributes are available for the Pane component:  export type PaneAttributes = {  /** Applied to every pane element. */  "data-pane": "";  /** The ID of the pane. */  "data-pane-id": string;  /** The ID of the pane's group. */  "data-pane-group-id": string;  /** The unit the pane is sized in. */  "data-units": "percentage" | "pixels"; }; `

title: Aligned Grids
description: An example of dividers that are dragged together while they line up.
content: import { AlignedGridsDemo } from '$lib/components/demos'  import ViewExampleCode from '$lib/components/view-example-code.svelte'   Drag the divider in either column. Both move, because they are on the same line.  The problem  Split a group into a 2x2 grid and each column keeps its own row sizes. The two row dividers start out looking like one line, but they are two separate things — drag either and they come apart.  The fix  Mark the group that holds the columns as align. Dividers in the groups nested inside it are then dragged together while they line up: two on the same line behave as one, and dragging either moves both.    import { PaneGroup, Pane, PaneResizer } from "paneforge";            One        Three                Two        Four        It works the same way round: mark a vertical group and the columns inside its rows line up instead.  What to expect  The groups stay independent. Nothing is shared and nobody's sizes are handed over. Each group keeps what you gave it, and onLayoutChange still reports its own sizes.  Only dividers that line up travel together. Two that sit on different lines have nothing to do with each other. This is worked out from where the dividers actually are each time a drag starts, so there is no state to keep in step.  They go as far as all of them can. Every move is offered to each of them and they all move by the smallest share any of them could manage, so a pair that started out as one line stays one line. When one reaches a pane's minSize, that is where both stop — the other does not run on and leave the line broken in two, whatever the panes on either side allow.  Double clicking evens out both. With evenOnDoubleClick, double clicking a linked divider evens out both of their groups, which leaves them on the same line.  It reaches one level. align links the dividers of the groups nested directly inside the marked group. Mark a nested group too if you want its own children linked.  Showing that they are linked  Two dividers that move as one should look like one, and a divider does not know from CSS alone what it is linked to — the other one is somewhere else entirely in the tree. So the resizer's child snippet hands you getLinkedIds(), the ids of the resizers that would come along:    {#snippet child({ props, junctions, getLinkedIds })}    (lit = [id, ...getLinkedIds()])}    onmouseleave={() => (lit = [])}    {@render junctions()}     {/snippet}   It is measured when called, so it answers for right now: two dividers that have come apart are no longer linked, and hovering either lights only itself.  Moving both axes at once  Where two dividers meet a third running across them, that corner is a $2 — dragging it moves every divider that meets there, along both axes. Junctions need no align: they appear wherever resizers touch.

title: Collapsible Panes
description: An example of how to create collapsible panes.
content: import { CollapsibleDemo } from '$lib/components/demos'  import ViewExampleCode from '$lib/components/view-example-code.svelte'   You can use the collapsedSize and collapsible props to create collapsible panes. The collapsedSize prop sets the size of the pane when it is in a collapsed state, and the collapsible prop determines whether the pane can be collapsed.  You can also use the onCollapse and onExpand callbacks to perform actions when the pane is collapsed or expanded, along with the pane prop to get a reference to the Pane component's API to programmatically collapse or expand the pane.  Anatomy  Here's the high-level structure of the example above:    import { PaneGroup, Pane, PaneResizer } from "paneforge";   let paneOne: ReturnType;  let collapsed = $state(false);   {#if collapsed}   Expand Pane One  {:else}   Collapse Pane One  {/if}    (collapsed = true)}   onExpand={() => (collapsed = false)}  />                          `

"Hide" : "Show"} Pane One   (showPaneThree = !showPaneThree)}>  {showPaneThree ? "Hide" : "Show"} Pane Three     {#if showPaneOne}        {/if}    {#if showPaneThree}        {/if}  `

title: Junctions
description: Resize a whole grid of nested panes from the point where their resizers meet.
content: import { JunctionsDemo } from '$lib/components/demos'  import ViewExampleCode from '$lib/components/view-example-code.svelte'   Drag any of the circles below. Each one moves the resizers that meet there at the same time, so both axes resize together.  The layout is nested four groups deep, and the single PaneJunctions in the outermost group covers all of it. The junction between Editor, Preview and Notes is formed by a resizer three levels down meeting one four levels down.  Anatomy  PaneJunctions finds the junctions itself and renders one element for each, so you never have to work out where they are or how many there are. Drop a single one into the outermost group and it covers everything nested inside it.    import { PaneGroup, Pane, PaneResizer, PaneJunctions } from "paneforge";  Styling the handle  Each junction is sized to the resizers it crosses, which keeps it from stealing room from them. To draw something larger, render your own element inside it — pointer events still reach the junction, so the visible handle doubles as the grab area.    {#snippet child({ props })}            {/snippet}   .junction-handle {  position: absolute;  top: 50%;  left: 50%;  width: 1.5rem;  height: 1.5rem;  transform: translate(-50%, -50%);  border-radius: 9999px;  background: var(--brand); }  Junctions come and go  A junction only exists while resizers actually meet. Drag Terminal's divider up to where the Explorer and Outline divider sits, and the two junctions on the middle resizer merge into a single cross that moves both. Pull them apart again and they split back into two.  Junctions that merely sit near each other stay independent: dragging one never moves the other, even where their hit areas overlap. Only resizers that actually line up are driven together.  You can tell the two apart with the data-junction-type attribute, which is cross when resizers meet the junction on both sides and tee when only one does:  $2 {  opacity: 0.5; } `

title: Persistent Layouts
description: Examples of persisting layouts across page loads.
content: import { StorageDemo, CookieDemo } from '$lib/components/demos'  import ViewExampleCode from '$lib/components/view-example-code.svelte'  import { page } from "$app/stores"  Local Storage  The PaneGroup component has an autoSaveId prop that can be used to uniquely identify the layout of the panes within the group. When provided, the layout of the panes will be saved to local storage and restored when the page is reloaded.  Anatomy  Here's the high-level structure of the example above:    import { PaneGroup, Pane, PaneResizer } from "paneforge";  Cookies (SSR-friendly)  Local storage is not available on the server, so you can use cookies to persist the layout of the panes across page loads, ensuring no layout flicker when the page is first loaded.  Anatomy  Here's the high-level structure of the example above:  import type { PageServerLoad } from "./$types";  export const load: PageServerLoad = async (event) => {  let layout = event.cookies.get("PaneForge:layout");  if (layout) {   layout = JSON.parse(layout);  }   return {   layout,  }; };    import { PaneGroup, Pane, PaneResizer } from "paneforge";   let { data } = $props();   function onLayoutChange(sizes: number[]) {   document.cookie = PaneForge:layout=${JSON.stringify(sizes)};  }           `

title: Pixel Sizes
description: An example of sizing a pane in pixels rather than as a share of the group.
content: import { PixelSizesDemo } from '$lib/components/demos'  import ViewExampleCode from '$lib/components/view-example-code.svelte'  Anatomy  Set units="pixels" on a pane and every size on it is read in pixels — defaultSize, minSize, maxSize, collapsedSize, and the sizes it reports back.    import { PaneGroup, Pane, PaneResizer } from "paneforge";     Sidebar    Content   That is the whole of it. The sidebar is 200px wide and stays 200px wide; the pane beside it is left alone, so it takes a share of the group and absorbs whatever changes.  What the two units mean  A share follows the group. A percentage pane takes its share of the group, so it grows and shrinks with it. This is the default, and a group of nothing but shares behaves exactly as it always has.  Pixels are absolute. A pixels pane keeps its size when the group changes size. Resize the window and the sidebar above is still 200px.  They are the two ways flexbox sizes a child, which is what lets them share a group: an absolute size becomes a flex-basis, taken out of the group first, and a share becomes a flex-grow weight over what is left.  Where the difference goes  When the group changes size, something has to give. It is offered to the panes taking a share first, split between them in proportion to what they already have, so their shares of one another are left alone.  Only what they cannot take is taken from the panes holding an absolute size, working backwards from the last. So a fixed sidebar gives way only once nothing else can — when the pane beside it has reached its own minSize, say — and is the last thing to be squeezed.  If no pane can give way at all, the sizes are scaled to fit as a last resort, so the panes always fill the group.  Limits in pixels  A size can name its own unit, whatever the pane is sized in. That matters most for minSize: a limit given as a share is a different number of pixels at every group size, so the same editor has a different smallest size at every nesting depth. In pixels it is the same everywhere, which is how VS Code behaves.    Editor    Terminal   Both panes here still take a share of the group, so they follow it as it resizes — they simply refuse to go below a width their contents need. maxSize and defaultSize read the same way, and "40%" works on a pane sized in pixels for the same reason in reverse.  If the group shrinks so far that a pane's pixel minimum no longer fits its share, the layout is pulled back to respect it — taking the space from whichever pane can give it.  A limit in pixels is also handed to flexbox, as a min-width or min-height on the pane along the axis its group runs. A share of the group has to make a round trip through a percentage to become pixels again, which leaves it a fraction of a pixel out; flex holds an item at its own minimum exactly, so a pane told it may not go below 48px measures 48px and not 48.02px.  One exception: a collapsible pane is given no floor, since its smallest size is its collapsedSize and a floor would stop it ever reaching it.  Percentages in a mixed group  A percentage is a share of the whole group, pixel panes included. So minSize={25} on the content pane above means a quarter of the group, which is a limit the sidebar will actually run into as it grows:    Sidebar    Content   The sizes onLayoutChange reports are each in that pane's own units, so the array above reads as [240, 75] — pixels for the sidebar, a share of the group for the content pane. getSize() on a pane and setLayout() on a group work the same way round.  Sizing a whole group in pixels  units on the group is the default for the panes inside it, for when every pane in a group should be measured the same way:    Top    Middle    The rest   A pane can still say otherwise for itself. Leaving the last pane without a defaultSize is how you say "take whatever is left over", in either unit.  Evening panes out  Double clicking a resize handle can give every pane in the group the same size. It is off unless you ask for it:       Every pane ends up the same size on screen, whichever unit each of them is written in. Double clicking a $2 does the same to every group it can move, so a crossing evens out along both axes at once.  The same thing is available as distributeEvenly() on the group, if you would rather put it behind a button or a keyboard shortcut:    import { PaneGroup } from "paneforge";   let group = $state(null!);    group.distributeEvenly()}>Even out      `
